Intel Foundry last week made available its Intel 14A process design kit (PDK) version 0.9, an important milestone in the development of this next-generation manufacturing technology. The company says that the production node is reaching performance and yield maturity expected at this stage of development, and the results are backed by silicon validation. Intel plans to release PDK 1.0 in the first quarter of 2027, which will validate the technology's readiness for high-volume manufacturing (HVM).

A process design kit contains transistor models, design rules, and other information that enables chip designers to develop products for a particular manufacturing process using electronic design automation (EDA) tools. The accuracy and quality of the PDK are crucial for modelling how chips will perform once manufactured, and the release of PDK 0.9 is particularly important because it provides customers with a representation of Intel 14A based on actual silicon measurements rather than on theoretical models or simulations. At this stage, customers can proceed with product development with greater confidence that the technology will meet their requirements when it comes to performance and power consumption.

Intel says that PDK 0.9 lets customers develop designs intended to enter risk production around the time the process is certified, which — provided that PDK accurately reflects the characteristics of manufactured silicon — in many cases enables chip developers to greatly reduce the number of silicon revisions between initial tapeout and mass production. Of course, availability of PDK 0.9 does not indicate that Intel 14A is ready or even close to mass production, as the company expects to validate HVM readiness only with PDK 1.0, sometime in Q1 2027. Again, this does not mean that 14A will enter mass production in early 2027, as Intel itself expects to begin mass production using its 14A process technology in 2028, following risk production for its own products in the second half of 2027.

"From a customer perspective, the PDK 0.9 gives customers the confidence to design products on Intel 14A, as the technology is reaching the industry-standard performance and yield maturity expected at this stage of development, supported by silicon-backed validation," said Ben Sell, corporate vice president and general manager of front-end technology development at Intel Foundry.

Intel 14A builds on top of architectural foundations introduced with Intel 18A but incorporates several substantial enhancements. These include 2nd Generation RibbonFET 2 gate-all-around (GAA) transistors, PowerDirect backside power delivery (which delivers power right to the transistor source/drain regions without using intermediate connections like TSVs used by PowerVia), and Turbo Cells (high-performance standard cells designed to accelerate timing-critical paths in CPUs and GPUs), which provide chip designers with additional ways to increase performance and optimize power efficiency. Since Intel has previously outlined advantages of these technologies, the latest announcement does not provide updates regarding transistor performance, power consumption, or transistor density figures for Intel 14A.

Beyond improvements to transistor, power delivery, and interconnect technologies, Intel is applying manufacturing experience gained during 12 months of Intel 18A production to accelerate maturation of 14A. Specifically, the company says it has increased investments in inline defect detection, modeling, and simulation to identify potential manufacturing problems earlier in the development cycle. These initiatives are intended to improve manufacturing yields, process variability, ultimately transistor performance, and reduce production cycle times. Intel also says it has introduced several strategic initiatives to accelerate technology development, although it does not quantify their impact.

Another important change concerns Intel's relationships with equipment and materials suppliers. The company says it has revised its collaboration model to involve technology development teams and external suppliers earlier in the process development cycle. The goal of such close collaborations is to address manufacturing defects and improve equipment capabilities before they become obstacles for yield improvements after the technology enters mass production. Intel also conducts regular yield summit meetings with suppliers to accelerate progress on critical development objectives.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

"This has required evolving our collaboration model with equipment and material suppliers, and earlier engagement from our [technology development] leaders with suppliers to drive improvements in defects and equipment capabilities," Sell said.

A bonus of such early collaboration is that equipment and materials suppliers may incorporate Intel's requirements into their standard products and development roadmaps. This could give Intel an advantage over competitors, which would have to either adapt their manufacturing processes to equipment optimized around Intel's requirements or work with suppliers to develop alternative solutions from scratch.

Historically, Intel frequently set the direction for semiconductor manufacturing technologies as other chipmakers subsequently adopted similar approaches. One notable exception was immersion DUV lithography, which Intel adopted after TSMC, which led the development of immersion DUV lithography. By engaging equipment and materials suppliers earlier, Intel could regain some of its historical influence over the development of industry-standard manufacturing solutions, though the importance of this should not be overestimated.

Meanwhile, Intel continues to expand the design ecosystem for its 14A technology. Cadence and Intel have established a design-technology co-optimization (DTCO) collaboration focused on next-generation AI-driven design tools and intellectual property, whereas Keysight, Siemens, and Synopsys have announced design-tool certifications for the process. Intel is also working with other software developers and IP providers to validate design flows and reusable building blocks required by prospective foundry customers.

Intel says it is encouraged by customer feedback regarding the progress of 14A development. However, the company has not identified any customers that have committed to manufacturing products using the technology, disclosed customer tape-outs, or announced specific manufacturing agreements, which is normal for the foundry industry. For Intel Foundry, attracting external customers remains particularly important because development costs of modern leading-edge process technologies can only be recoupled when they are used to make hundreds of millions of chips, way more than Intel sells these days. Meanwhile, the commercial success of Intel Foundry with advanced manufacturing technologies depends not only on transistor performance and manufacturing yields, but also on its ability to deliver predictable development schedules.

Looking ahead, Intel intends to continue improving performance, yields, variability, and manufacturing cycle times of 14A, though for now the company does not disclose any actual goals. Intel also plans additional process enhancements and performance refinements for 14A-E and 14A-P nodes after the initial technology becomes available. However, exact schedules for these nodes are not known at the moment.

"Our next major milestone is the Intel 14A PDK 1.0, expected in the first quarter of 2027," said Ali Farhang, corporate vice president and general manager of Intel Foundry's design technology platform organization. "I am looking forward to sustaining this level of quality across future releases and continuing to earn our customers' trust by delivering on our commitments with a customer-first mindset."

At the Android Dev Summit 2026 earlier this week, Google said that Googlebook detachables will be the next form factor after clamshells and convertibles.

#10652. Bad memory: Some chip stocks are tumbling despite the broader post-election rally for tech. Here’s why

Tuesday’s blue tsunami didn’t just boost the Democrats’ fortunes. The 2026 midterm results also fueled a surge in the stock market, with all but a few Big Tech stocks seeing notable gains. 

But memory chip stocks told a different story. Shares in the four major memory chipmakers all saw steep declines. And those declines are continuing today. Here’s what you need to know.

The midterm results boosted the markets

Yesterday was a stellar day for many of the biggest-name companies traded on the markets. And a stellar day for the markets in general. As CNN noted, the Dow had its best post-midterm-election day in 44 years, with a jump of about 3%, or 1,569 points.

The S&P 500 jumped 1.58%, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq was up 1.44%.

When it comes to individual stocks, Big Tech (mostly) had a great day.

Microsoft Corporation (Nasdaq: MSFT) ended the day up 6.6%, Apple Inc. (Nasdaq: AAPL) rose 5.3%, Amazon.com, Inc. (AMZN) jumped 6.1%, Netflix, Inc. (Nasdaq: NFLX) rose 4.6%, Alphabet Inc. (Nasdaq: GOOG) was up 3.2%, and Meta Platforms, Inc. (Nasdaq: META) was up 1.4%. 

As of the time of this writing, all those companies are continuing to see gains in premarket trading this morning, too.

The main reason for the stock market’s big day yesterday was the certainty brought by the Democrats’ decisive victory. There is no question about which party will hold the levers of power in Congress when its members are sworn in in January. Investors hate uncertainty, and the Democrats’ historic win all but eliminated it.

Memory chipmakers left out of the rally

Despite the broader gains, yesterday was not a good day for one type of company in particular: memory chipmakers.

Micron Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: MU) saw its stock sink 7%, SanDisk Corporation (Nasdaq: SNDK) fell 7.9%, Western Digital Corporation (Nasdaq: WDC) dropped 6.7%, and Seagate Technology Holdings plc(Nasdaq: STX) fell a staggering 8.1%.

And yes, the election results were likely to blame for those drops, too.

Unfortunately for investors in memory chip companies, yesterday’s massive drop in memory chip shares doesn’t seem to be a one-off. In premarket trading this morning, memory stocks are once again getting hammered, as of the time of this writing.

  • Micron Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: MU): down nearly 4%
  • SanDisk Corporation (Nasdaq: SNDK): down 5.3%
  • Western Digital Corporation (Nasdaq: WDC): down 4.7%
  • Seagate Technology Holdings plc (Nasdaq: STX): down 4.5%

Why are memory chip stocks falling?

The main worry investors seem to have is that the midterm election results weren’t just a referendum on the Republican Party, which currently controls Congress, and the Trump administration. 

Yes, Americans punished both for rising prices and an unpopular war, but another issue was also top of mind in many state and local elections: data centers.

Many of the Democrats who won those elections ran on an anti-AI and anti-data center stance, promising either moratoriums or restrictions on the building of the unpopular server farms that are popping up across the country.

And now many of those Democrats hold the levers of power not just in Washington, but also locally, where the data centers are being built.

Any reining in of the data center expansion is bad news for memory chipmakers.

Data centers need servers to run AI, and those servers need massive amounts of RAM. If data center buildouts slow, the demand for RAM shrinks at a commensurate rate. And that’s bad for memory chipmakers’ bottom lines.

Voters are unified in their opposition to data centers

There are few issues that both the left and right can agree on, but one of them is their dislike for data centers.

As noted by Reuters, an NBC and SSRS exit poll revealed that around 76% of voters opposed new data centers being built where they lived.

Those voters just sent a massive blue wave to Washington, and that doesn’t bode well for an increased data center buildout.

“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Elon Musk quipped, alluding to the opposition that terrestrial data centers now face.

Other billionaires were more foreboding.

As noted by CNBC, billionaire investor Chamath Palihapitiya warned that “the only way to sink the AI trade is to sink the data centers.”

Pershing Square founder Bill Ackman warned that slowing AI development could put America’s tech advantage in danger, declaring, “Practically speaking, we can’t slow down.”

Yet given the sinking stock prices of memory chip and storage makers, a slowdown is exactly what investors seem to think is coming.

Earlier this week, Google revealed that a “later platform release of Wear OS” is adding a “system status bar.”

On October 26, Google released a Wear OS canary emulator in Android Studio to let developers “test upcoming platform features and user interface changes before they become available in a consumer platform release on physical devices.”

The upcoming feature in question is a “persistent system status bar over Wear OS app windows at the top position of the circular display.” It will display the “current time and system status indicators,” similar to Android on phones and tablets.

Additionally: “These indicators use standardized clock typography, placement, and backplate across the platform and different apps, including your app.” Apps that require a fullscreen experience will be able to hide the status bar.

As of this preview, “the system status bar displays a placeholder star icon instead of final system status indicators.”

This emulator is published as Wear OS 7.1 (API level 37.2-beta1, based on Android 17 “CinnamonBun”) with a CP41.260831.001.E8 build ID. This reveals that Wear OS 7.1 is coming, but it sounds like the status bar will launch in a later release: “The system status bar is included exclusively in this canary emulator to support early testing and feedback. It won’t be included in the upcoming Wear OS 7.1 stable emulator.”

This move could help data centers operate sooner without waiting for the rest of the grid to catch up to its peak demand.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Electricity consumption is one of the biggest concerns that residents bring up whenever a data center is proposed in their community, which is why OpenAI is taking steps to minimize its impact on the local electricity grid. According to the company, its Grid Protectors Program aims to reduce the power consumption of its data centers as local demand increases, ensuring that the grid is not overwhelmed during peak hours. Aside from ensuring that the lights remain on for everyone, it would also allow its data centers to connect to the grid and go online sooner instead of waiting for the additional power sources to come online.

“Whether it’s heating homes during a northern cold snap or running air conditioning through a southern heat wave, families need reliable electricity. Our goal is to make campus flexibility a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most,” OpenAI said in its blog. It also added, “Through Grid Protectors, our ambition is to make this kind of flexibility a core part of how we build and operate future campuses. That means designing facilities to reduce electricity use when needed and working with utilities to agree on how much demand can be reduced, how quickly and for how long. The arrangements will differ by location, and we will share additional commitments as they are finalized.”

OpenAI is testing the program in its planned Effingham County campus in Georgia, with the company saying that it has already signed a 3.2-gigawatt agreement with Georgia Power that included 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response. This ensures that if demand jumps on the hottest days of the year, there would be enough power to accommodate the hundreds of thousands of air conditioners keeping Georgians cool. With the average American home drawing around 1,200 kilowatts, the 1,000-megawatt buffer is more than enough to power around 800,000 households — nearly 20% of the state’s homes.

This technology, called demand response, has been around for decades now, where large operators reduce their demand in response to a peak in demand from other consumers. Before automation, grid operators would manually call up industrial customers like steel mills and ask them to cut consumption to ensure the reliability of the entire grid. But with modern technologies and IoT, it can now be done automatically, allowing data centers to reduce their load in under a minute. In fact, Nvidia has already been experimenting with a similar system in the UK and has proven that it works.

#10647. What is Trump’s next move on his unpopular Iran war, now that the midterms are over?

As he takes stock of his Republican Party’s midterm drubbing, President Donald Trump now faces the difficult question of what to do about his unpopular 8-month-old war against Iran.

For weeks, Trump has threatened to return to a full-scale bombardment of Iran once the U.S. elections were in the rearview mirror if Tehran did not come to a settlement under terms acceptable to him.

In his first comments on Wednesday after Democrats’ resounding election victory — a wave powered in part by the American electorate’s dissatisfaction with the war — Trump largely agreed with Vice President JD Vance, who publicly ruminated on the war being a catastrophe for Republicans.

“It’s largely true because it drove gasoline up a little bit,” Trump said. Still, he doubled down on his decision to launch the conflict despite its big political cost. “At the same time, if I had to do it again, I’d do it again,” he said.

The strikes, and counterstrikes, have caused tens of billions of dollars of damage in the region. And the conflict has reached into the pocketbook of families around the globe with elevated gas prices and rising costs in just about every sector.

Now, as Trump ponders his next move, the stakes couldn’t be higher for Iran, the Middle East and the global economy writ large.

Trump may be less restrained, but the conflict is now more complicated

While oil is flowing again from the Strait of Hormuz with the help of U.S. Navy escorts for international tankers, the conflict has spread to the Red Sea with Iran-backed Houthi rebels and a Saudi Arabia-led coalition fighting it out.

The situation in the Red Sea remains particularly volatile. The Houthis are attacking Yemeni civilians and Saudi infrastructure, and are looking to bolster ties with militant groups across the Horn of Africa.

The attacks by the Yemen-based Houthis on areas controlled by the internationally recognized Yemeni government have also worsened a growing humanitarian crisis.

The threat that the region faces from Iran and its proxy groups, noted a senior Yemeni government official, “did not change overnight” with the U.S. elections, urging Washington to avoid hasty decisions. The official was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the basis of anonymity.

“There’s reason to suspect that Trump may feel less restrained given that the political damage is done,” said Brian Haggerty, a former senior analyst at the Central Intelligence Agency who focused on Middle East security issues. “At the same time, the strategic calculus or the strategic logic of what you hope to achieve through an escalation of strikes against Iran is no different today than it was a week ago or a month ago.”

Trump has at least a few options, analysts say

Haggerty, who now works with Defense Priorities, a Washington think tank, said Trump could choose to maintain something close to the current posture, with the U.S. military carrying out what it calls “defensive strikes” while continuing its naval blockade to restrict the flow of Iranian oil to the global market.

Another option is striking Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to its nuclear program that is buried deep underground in central Iran, said David Schenker, who served as assistant secretary of state for Near Eastern affairs in Trump’s first term. Trump has repeatedly suggested he was considering targeting the site.

Schenker said Trump could then walk away and contend he had done sufficient damage to Iran’s nuclear program — and perhaps try to pursue a “fig leaf agreement” that restores freedom of navigation to the Strait of Hormuz, offers Iran some degree of sanctions relief, and punts additional nuclear talks to the future.

Yet another option would be to follow up on threats Trump made earlier in the war to launch massive attacks on Iranian infrastructure. “The Iranians may believe the president is wounded and constrained by Congress, but the opposite can also be true,” Schenker said.

But such escalation would likely exacerbate the oil and energy price problem that many voters cited as a reason for supporting Democrats on Tuesday, Schenker said.

The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil tumbled below $95 on Wednesday after the election, touching its lowest level in two months, a signal that markets do not expect major strikes.

Regional officials are on high alert for what Trump does next

Middle East officials had been hanging on Trump’s every word in the weeks leading up to the U.S. elections, looking for clues on how the Republican leader was weighing his next steps.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed for renewed strikes on Iran during a call over the weekend with Trump, who would not commit to taking military action, according to a person who was briefed on it.

Three Middle Eastern government officials said on Wednesday that Trump and his administration had seemed to be signaling to Iran that its leverage would only diminish after the U.S. elections were over.

Administration officials had privately suggested in diplomatic channels that Trump might be more willing to restart strikes after Nov. 3 because he’d have little left to lose politically, according to the officials, who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.

After Tuesday’s electoral shellacking, there was lingering concern that Trump might be more emboldened to carry out full-scale or new limited strikes against Iran, the officials said.

A fourth official said the results of the election gave mediators a measure of optimism about finding a pathway to resolving the conflict.

Meanwhile, Vance appeared to more forcefully pin the electoral debacle on the Iran war than his boss Trump, who initially blamed the GOP’s candidates for the big loss.

“The reason we lost,” Vance said of the midterm elections in a lengthy social media post, “is the war.”

Vance, a potential 2028 presidential contender, had been among the most skeptical inside the White House on the wisdom of launching the war but got on board with Trump’s decision once he made it.

Voter data shows Iran had an impact but was not the top issue

Several Democratic candidates who scored upsets on Tuesday noted voter discontent with the Iran war in their victory speeches.

“Wherever I went, I heard the same thing,” said Sen.-elect Josh Turek of Iowa. “They would say, Josh, I’m struggling just to keep food on the table, keep a roof above my head, pay my electric bill. And with this war in Iran, I’m struggling just to keep gas in my tank.”

About 6 in 10 voters said the U.S. made the “wrong decision” in taking military action against Iran, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters in the United States.

Most of those voters dissatisfied with the Iran war backed the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race, but the survey suggested the Iran war was not the top issue for most voters.

Only about one-third of voters said the war in Iran was “crucial” to shaping how they voted for Congress. That was well below the roughly half who said that about the cost of living or government corruption.

Nearly all voters who backed the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race said going to war with Iran was the “wrong decision,” while roughly 8 in 10 voters who backed the Republican candidate said it was the “right decision.”

Meanwhile, about 6 in 10 voters nationally said they were “very concerned” about the cost of gasoline and diesel, the poll showed — and about two-thirds of that group voted for the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race.

But Trump, for his part, said even in hindsight he’d approach Iran exactly as he has.

“I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned I would have done nothing different,” the president said.

AP writers Collin Binkley, Hannah Fingerhut, and Kathleen Foody contributed reporting.

—Aamer Madhani, Linley Sanders, Samy Magdy and Matthew Lee, Associated Press

#10644. The blue heart is the unofficial emoji of libbing out

The blue heart emoji is having a moment among those celebrating Democrats’ midterm election results, and while you can clock this in many a comments section, it’s also backed up by stats.

Tinashe, the pop star, used the emoji 12 times in a post on X on Election Day encouraging her fans to vote, writing, “VOTE OR DIE ! LETS GO AMERICA 💙💙💙💙💙💙💙💙💙💙💙💙,” and others have spammed the emoji too in posts “libbing out” in excitement over the midterm results.

Scroll through the comments section on the Democratic Party’s official Instagram account (which posted on the grid nearly 100 times in 24 hours with good news of flipped states and seats) and you’ll see a tsunami of blue hearts. It’s occasionally paired with other emoji expressing joy, like for clapping hands, the U.S. flag, or a wave.

Google searches for the emoji are up 80% from last month, and up 1,050% from the comparable period last year, and they’re highest in Texas and North Carolina, two states where Democrats flipped U.S. House and Senate seats. On Emojitracker, which tracks real-time emoji copies on Emojipedia and GetEmoji, the blue heart emoji outpaced the pink and white hearts by more than two to one on Wednesday. (The red heart emoji, which is used more generally as the standard heart color for love, is the top emoji on the platform.)

Emojis have been adopted to signify political movements or support before, like the emoji for the rose, a longtime socialist symbol that Democratic Socialists of America uses in tweets. During Kamala Harris’s 2024 presidential campaign, her supporters used coconut and palm tree emoji to refer to her widely memed comments about context, and last year, Canada’s Green Party adopted the green dot emoji as its new logo.

Using the color blue for the left-of-center party is a uniquely American quirk of visual political communications. In other western democracies, the colors are flipped, and red is associated with movements ranging from labor to socialism and communism. Mainstream center-left parties like the U.K.’s Labour Party and Canada’s Liberal Party use red as their primary color, while the Conservative parties in both countries are associated with blue.

Before 2000, the colors used to represent a party depended on the TV network, news outlet, and year. But after the weeks-long recount in Florida of the 2000 presidential race between George W. Bush and Al Gore, which played out over cable news and nightly newscasts, the networks standardized the current color schemes, which stuck.

In 2004, the Republican Party formalized red as its color when it rebranded to an all-red “GOP” logo, and during his speech at that year’s Democratic National Convention, Barack Obama, then a senator from Illinois, bemoaned pundits who “like to slice and dice our country into red states and blue states.”

Though the colors had caught on as shorthand for the contemporary partisan divide of conservative rural areas and liberal urban areas, Obama still explained which party stood for which color during his 2004 speech, for listeners who might not be familiar with the terminology. Today, it’s so widely understood that the Democratic Party’s social media posts simply referred to their candidates either keeping or flipping a seat to “blue,” and a string of blue emojis can communicate excitement over Democrats’ big night without saying a word.

Writing HTML is one of the main parts of building a website. It is mainly responsible for webpage structure and content.

A small error can result in layout problems. Oftentimes, you don't notice these issues until you preview the page in a browser. A quick way to ensure that your layout looks the same as you want is to preview your HTML code.

In this blog, we’ll show you easy ways to check how your HTML code will look in real time. So keep on reading till the end.

The following are two easy ways to check how your HTML code will look in real time.

This is a simple way to preview your HTML. You don't need a web server to preview your HTML code. You have to follow the following steps.

Open a code editor or simply Notepad on your device. Create a new file and paste your HTML inside it.

Step 2 - Save the File With an HTML Extension

After adding your HTML code in Notepad, save the file as index.html. You have to ensure that the extension is .html, not .txt.

If you are using Notepad on Windows, click on “File” and navigate to the “Save As” option and click it. Then enter index.html as the filename. Make sure that Notepad doesn’t save it as a text document.

Locate the saved file on your device. Double-click to open it in your default browser. The browser will render the HTML elements to show the headings, paragraphs, and buttons on the page, as you can see in the image below.

This is how you can create a simple file to preview your HTML before deploying it. If you see any errors, you can correct them in your file and preview it again.

However, it is worth considering that HTML may not show the complete website behavior alone. The final result can also depend on JavaScript, external CSS, or other resources. You should check those files as well.

This method provides an easy way to preview your HTML code. It involves using a specialized online HTML viewer. This approach is even quicker and doesn't even require you to create a local file first.

Step 1 - Open the HTML Viewer Open your web browser and search for an HTML viewer. You may see multiple tools in the search results. Select one that allows HTML preview online. For demonstration purposes, we are using HTML Viewer by minifier.org.

Once you’ve selected the tool, open it. Navigate to its input box and paste your HTML code into it. We are using the same HTML code from the first example.

You can also upload your file or paste its URL into the tool. After entering your HTML code, click on the “View” button to preview your HTML code.

In the screenshot above, you can see the tool showing the HTML preview on the right side. This tool also gives you the option to edit your HTML code and see the results in real time through the “Auto-update” option.

If the auto-update option is checked, you can see the changes in real time as you edit the code. This makes editing much easier, as you can modify the code and preview the changes immediately without returning to your original file. It also allows you to verify how your layout will appear on desktop, tablet, or mobile. You can check this by clicking on the icons provided in the top right corner of the tool. Once you are satisfied with the output, you can copy or download your edited HTML file easily.

This tool also allows you to test the HTML code of your game or video in real time, as you can see in the screenshot below.

These features make such specialized HTML viewers practical. These are quick and easy to use. However, the features shown above may not be available on all the tools. If you are specifically looking for such features, you can read the tool’s description for these features before using it.

HTML is one of the main components of a website. It defines the structure and content of webpages. Many users need to check how their HTML code will look in a browser to identify potential issues before deployment.

To preview your HTML code, you can use simple methods. One is to paste your code into Notepad and save it as index.html. Then open it in your browser to get a preview of your HTML code.

You can also use a specialized HTML viewer. Such tools can work by just pasting the code into the input box. Once you paste your code, click on the view button to get a preview of your HTML code. Some tools also offer various other features, such as editing, viewing games, and videos in real time.

Both of these methods work fine. The choice depends on the user's preferences and needs.

Following a resurgence of 8GB RAM laptops earlier this year, and in the wake of promises to improve Windows 11 performance using just 8GB of RAM, Microsoft has today announced what it claims are a series of performance improvements. Driven by an ongoing global PC component shortage that is forcing manufacturers to dumb down specs, the company says that with 8GB of RAM, Windows is now 20% more responsive and 40% faster when it comes to multitasking.

The development shared today by Microsoft is an update to a commitment earlier this year to improve the quality and performance of Windows 11, a major bugbear of users since its launch. Microsoft says it has taken a three-pronged approach to memory optimization: making better use of memory in Windows 11 PCs, protecting interactions that need to feel instant, and ensuring key apps and Windows use less memory. While the company admits you'll be able to do more on 16GB or 32GB of RAM, it says "we're making sure you can do more, even with 8GB."

The headline performance gain is a claim that Windows is now up to 20% more responsive on 8GB PCs. Likewise, multitasking is now purportedly 40% faster in Microsoft's lab tests. Of course, these are internal tests conducted in favorable conditions by Microsoft.

Microsoft says it has tuned compression for useful apps and data, and can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory, rather than moving it to storage. In practice, this should mean that apps and tabs left open should be less likely to reload when you go back to them.

The claim of 20% more responsiveness specifically relates to tasks like opening Start, searching, right-clicking, opening Settings, using the Snipping Tool, and opening File Explorer. The company says it has achieved this by backing off background tasks like indexing while you're using your PC actively. Edge now reportedly opens up to 33% faster. There's also an Efficiency Mode for Microsoft Teams, which can be set to on by default, improving launch times by 20%.

Microsoft says that its claims of 40% speed boosts to multitasking are based on a demanding workflow of 20 Microsoft Edge Tabs, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, Outlook, and File Explorer all being opened one after the other.

Other improvements include reducing committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB in apps like Microsoft Edge and 365 apps, and reducing the memory footprint of Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook by 360MB. Third-party apps can also benefit from improved memory management, with Microsoft stating WhatsApp is already taking advantage.

Moving forward, Microsoft says it has plans to make memory compression even smarter and more efficient. Windows features and apps will share common parts, such as Search and Widgets using one web Engine, for instance. WinUI 3 apps like File Explorer and Notepad will be designed to use less memory and open faster, and Microsoft is working with PC makers and silicon manufacturers to reduce how much memory a PC needs to hold in reserve to support its hardware, making more space for Windows.

#10639. Chase Sapphire Reserve is making a major change to its luxury travel perks in 2027

Chase is giving its premium credit cardholders a new way to use their travel benefits for stays: vacation homes.

Starting January, Chase Travel will expand The Edit, its curated collection of luxury hotels and resorts, to include more than 10,000 vacation home properties. The homes will join the more than 1,500 hotels and resorts already in the collection, giving eligible cardholders more options for using their annual travel credits.

Thursday’s announcement comes alongside new survey findings that suggest travelers are increasingly planning vacations around credit card rewards, group experiences, and opportunities to learn something new.

In an interview with Fast Company, Chase Travel’s CEO, Jason Wynn, said the move reflects changing traveler preferences, particularly among younger consumers and people planning vacations with larger groups.

“We’ve actually been in the vacation home business for a little while,” Wynn said. “We launched vacation home rentals on Chase travel last year.”

The company added properties from Plum Guide, a selective vacation rental platform, earlier this year and has seen growing interest from cardholders. For Chase, the expansion is part of a broader effort to make its travel platform useful for more types of trips, whether that means a luxury hotel, a private house on the beach, or something else.

Chase Sapphire Reserve cardholders are getting new vacation rental perks

The new vacation houses will be available through The Edit to Chase Sapphire Reserve, Sapphire Reserve for Business, and J.P. Morgan Reserve cardmembers.

Unlike booking a typical vacation rental through a platform like Airbnb, eligible home stays will come with some of the benefits travelers might typically associate with luxury hotels. For instance, cardmembers will receive a $150 in-stay credit that can be used toward experiences and services such as massages, private chefs, and airport transportation. Properties will also offer perks like early check-in and late checkout when the property can accommodate them.

There’s an important catch: To take advantage of those benefits you’ll have to book a minimum four-night stay.

These also aren’t your regular run-of-the-mill vacation properties. The homes are being curated in partnership with Plum Guide, which evaluates properties against more than 150 criteria covering comfort, design, and location.

When they go to make a booking, Chase Sapphire Reserve cardmembers will have access to Reserve Travel Designers, a 24/7 concierge service that can help match travelers with properties and provide assistance before, during, and after their stays.

Wynn said the goal isn’t to replace luxury hotels with vacation rentals, but instead to offer its customers a larger variety of options that match the reason they’re traveling.

“I don’t think it’s either or a situation. I think hotels and vacation homes fundamentally serve different needs, and we’re starting to see consumers increasingly want access to both,” he said.

For instance, a hotel might be the better choice for a couple taking a long weekend, while a private home might be better for a multigenerational family vacation or a weeklong trip with friends.

The expansion also creates another way for cardholders to use their annual Edit credits.

Personal Sapphire Reserve cardmembers can receive up to $500 in annual statement credits for eligible stays through The Edit. Beginning January 1, Sapphire Reserve for Business cardmembers can receive up to $1,000 annually, with a maximum of $250 per stay.

Qualifying bookings must be prepaid and include at least two nights at a participating hotel property. Travelers hoping to receive the additional vacation home benefits, however, will need to stay at least four nights.

Chase isn’t limiting vacation rental bookings to its most expensive cards. Freedom, Ink Business Preferred, and Sapphire Preferred cardmembers can also book from hundreds of thousands of vacation home properties through Chase Travel, although those reservations don’t necessarily include The Edit’s premium benefits.

Credit card rewards are changing how people book travel

Chase’s vacation rental expansion arrives as its own research suggests travelers are making rewards a bigger part of their vacation planning.

In a survey of 4,082 travelers and diners, conducted between August 31 and September 8, 2026, nearly half of respondents (48%) said travel was a primary way they redeemed rewards. 

Rewards aren’t just helping travelers pay for trips. They’re also influencing the decisions people make along the way. Some 51% of respondents said rewards have influenced their hotel choices, and 50% said the same about airlines. Another 41% of respondents said rewards have affected the type of room or airline cabin they book, and for 28%, rewards have influenced whether they take a trip at all.

Wynn gave another detail about how customers are paying for their bookings.

“One of the more interesting things we’re seeing is that more than half of transactions on Chase travel are now paid in cash rather than points,” he said.

He said that wasn’t the case a year ago, suggesting customers are increasingly using the platform even when they aren’t redeeming rewards.

At the same time, Chase’s survey found that 57% of respondents would rather use saved points to reduce travel costs when prices rise than pay cash and continue accumulating rewards. Chase has been investing in benefits such as Points Boost, which can make points worth up to twice as much on select travel bookings, and a price match guarantee.

For Chase, the goal is to persuade customers to book through its platform regardless of whether they’re paying with cash or rewards. Wynn said the company is already seeing significant growth in overall travel demand, with Chase Travel bookings up 14% year over year.

Another trend Chase expects to see more of in 2027 is the rise of the “craftcation,” a trip built around learning something new. Nearly seven in 10 travelers (69%) said they were interested in vacations centered on learning or developing a skill.

According to Wynn, the definition of luxury itself is evolving as travelers increasingly prioritize memorable experiences like a cooking class over the traditional markers of an expensive vacation.

“I think luxury has always been about the experience, but what’s changing is how people define a great experience,” he said.

That thinking extends beyond hotels and vacation rentals. Wynn said Chase’s online cruise booking business, launched last spring, has become its fastest-growing travel segment, with triple-digit growth this year. The company has also expanded its travel advisory services and continues to invest in more personalized trip planning.

“Ultimately, we want Chase Travel to be a place people choose because it’s the best way for them to travel,” not just because it’s where they can use their points, Wynn said.

#10637. 100,000 polled voters delivered a midterm verdict on Trump’s economy. Here are 4 takeaways

President Donald Trump was publicly humbled by inflation in the midterm elections, as rising prices provoked a blistering set of losses for Republicans in House, Senate and gubernatorial races.

Most voters said that Trump’s own policies had smothered growth and driven costs even higher, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of roughly 100,000 midterm voters. The president’s message that the fault lay with his predecessor, Democrat Joe Biden, didn’t land. Americans saw prices start to climb with Trump’s chaotic rash of tariffs last year, and energy costs spiked after he launched a war with Iran in February.

About two-thirds of voters said Trump’s own policies had fueled inflation. By contrast, only about half of 2022 midterm voters said this about Biden’s policies, according to AP VoteCast.

Voters in states from California to Mississippi were broadly in agreement that Trump’s taxes on foreign imports have done more harm than good.

The election results matched what voters had been telling pollsters for months, but Trump had campaigned with a decidedly deaf ear.

“I’ve done a great job,” Trump said at one of his final midterm rallies in Iowa. “Prices are coming way down.”

Voters have buyer’s remorse with Trump

Democratic victories in Tuesday’s midterms signaled that most voters don’t believe the economy or Trump is working for them.

Consumer prices are up 3.7% over the past 12 months, compared to an inflation rate of 3% when Trump began his second term. The president told reporters on Wednesday that the Iran war “drove the gasoline up a little bit short-term,” but he felt the choice to fight Iran was worth it because of its push for nuclear weapons. “If I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again,” he said.

There is no guarantee that a House and Senate with a Democratic majority can fix an economy pestered by uncomfortably high inflation. Trump and Congress would likely need to work on a bipartisan basis, or simply keep the economy stable enough to allow the Federal Reserve to ratchet down inflation through its setting of interest rates.

But voters did prefer Democrats to the status quo of a president who could govern with little to no congressional pushback from Republicans.

About 9 in 10 voters said the cost of living was a “crucial” or “major” factor in their vote for Congress. And about 6 in 10 of this group backed Democratic candidates in their local House races.

The economy is still growing, but AI is a source of fear instead of hope

The underlying economy is stronger than many Americans think, with the S&P 500 stock index up more than 10% so far this year and the unemployment rate at a healthy 4.2%. Investors greeted the news of Democratic wins as a positive with stocks up on Wednesday.

Still, the major driver of growth has been the buildout of artificial intelligence — a boom that Trump has actively stoked by refusing to codify more aggressive federal oversight.

Voters don’t share Trump’s optimism about AI, which he has renamed “super intelligence” in federal documents.

Instead of buying the arguments that AI would increase productivity and accelerate growth, about 6 in 10 voters said AI will do more to hurt society.

The technology could displace workers as jobs get automated or it could be a financial bubble that if popped could wreak havoc on retirement savings. Despite the anxiety, only about one-quarter of voters said AI was a “crucial” factor.

Wealth isn’t trickling down to the middle class

Tech billionaires such as Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Elon Musk have become frequent guests of Trump, attending state dinners or jetting abroad with the president. But the growing concentration of wealth has been disconcerting for voters.

Nationwide, about 7 in 10 voters said the economy favors wealthy people, while only about 3 in 10 said it’s fair to everyday Americans. The wealth gap has become so extreme that even a majority of voters with a 2025 household income of $300,000 or more in the tech-heavy state of California felt the economy was tilted toward the rich.

Still, a slight majority of voters across the country had a “somewhat” or “very” favorable impression of capitalism, compared to about one-third who “strongly” or “somewhat” favor socialism.

But the election suggested that voters believe the government should use its heft to help reduce the cost of healthcare. About 6 in 10 said they wanted the government to play a “bigger role” in addressing medical expenses. Most voters said Trump’s policies have made healthcare costs worse.

Trump caught in a trap with voters

How voters felt about the overall economy generally depended on the size of their paychecks. While Trump campaigned on stats suggesting record low poverty, the working poor saw their own finances as crumbling.

For those earning less than $50,000 a year, about 6 in 10 said they were worse off now than they were two years ago before Trump became president.

People with higher incomes felt better about the economy, but that created a different problem for Trump. Higher-income voters were more concerned about the state of American democracy, and voters focused on democracy overwhelmingly broke for Democrats. Without congressional approval, Trump laid off thousands of federal workers, altered federal spending and imposed hundreds of billions of dollars in new tariffs that the Supreme Court earlier this year ruled were illegal.

About 4 in 10 households with 2025 household incomes above $200,000 said that democracy was their top issue, putting the issue about even with the economy. Voters in most lower-income categories, on the other hand, clearly prioritized the economy.

Overall, a slim majority of voters said government corruption was a crucial factor for their vote, while about half said this about high prices. Higher-income voters were much less likely than lower-income voters to see high prices as a key factor.

What most voters took away from the past 22 months of Trump’s presidency was that he brokered deals, took government stakes in private companies and acted in ways that put him at the center of the economy instead of America’s workers.

Most voters — about 6 in 10 — said Trump’s priorities were misplaced.

When voters were asked if Trump fought for people like them, most said he didn’t.

The AP Voter Poll is a survey of more than 100,000 voters conducted by SSRS for The Associated Press, ABC News, CBS News, CNN, FOX News Media, NBC News and Versant. The survey blends probability-based and non-probability-based interviews with registered voters in all 50 states conducted from Oct. 19 to Nov. 3 in Alaska and Oct. 22 to Nov. 3 in all other states. A detailed methodology statement is available here. The margin of sampling error is plus or minus 0.6 percentage points for the full sample.

—Josh Boak, Associated Press

#10635. Gemini 4 Carbon lags just behind Claude in benchmark, but wins in value

Google’s new frontier model, Gemini 4 Carbon, brings some welcome improvements and while it doesn’t top the charts in a new benchmark, it does provide much more bang for your buck.

SemiAnalysis, an AI research and analysis firm, recently published its new frontier-level benchmark, GDPx which includes numbers for Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon model. The leaderboard includes every major frontier model from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta and details both the score and cost for each model.

The benchmark includes 206 tasks across finance, materials science, cybersecurity, software engineering, legal, biology, and several other domains (topics).

Topping the results is Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, but Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon is very close behind. The difference between the two is relatively minimal, but the cost is the biggest factor to consider here. Where Claude’s cost came out to around $51 per task, Gemini was just over $16 per task. Gemini also beat the next model on the list, GPT-6 Astra, which scored lower while costing more than both at about $54 per task.

The report notes that taking out cybersecurity, biology, and alignment domains shuffles the results. Safety guardrails in Claude and GPT models puts GPT-6 Astra at the top of the list with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5 outranking Gemini 4 Carbon. SemiAnalysis says that this better aligns with their “subjective impressions” of each model.

As for Google’s existing frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, it ranks in eighth place on both lists, beating Meta’s Muse Wonder, but below Wonder Full. Argon’s costs in this particular benchmark are only slightly lower than Carbon.

Both of Google’s models score better than OpenAI and Anthropic models when focused on cybersecurity, but do fall behind Meta’s Muse models, which the benchmark found to be the best “by a meaningful margin.”

Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28 and touted “significant gains,” but the public release date has not been confirmed just yet. It is “coming soon” for most customers. Google’s own benchmark, below, beat GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 in many aspects.

The engine drives a 400v motor-generator that electrically drives the propellers.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers at U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) Army Research Laboratory (ARL) recently successfully flew the VICTOR hybrid electric drone with a heavy-fuel rotary engine, rapidly developed thanks to metal 3D printing — allowing the drone to extract more performance out of the denser but less volatile military fuel source.

The heavy fuel (JP8) used in the drone is a denser kerosene-based fuel source compared to regular jet fuel, making it desirable to reduce total fuel load or increase mileage. The JP8 fuel is part of the military’s initiative to power as much of its gas equipment on a single fuel source. However, JP8 is less volatile and harder to atomize, making it a challenge to achieve peak efficiency. Furthermore, the fuel’s flash point is 140℉, compared to gasoline’s -40℉, requiring the engine to have a much higher compression to ignite it, making pressure leaks a common issue.

JP-8 fuel on aircraft and drones is not uncommon; however, the ARL researchers wanted to further optimize the heavy-fuel rotary engine to extract more performance and improve its design. The researchers used computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and a clean-sheet design (designing from scratch, essentially), allowing the engineers to come up with more innovative solutions to get more out of the engine with less.

"The use of advanced manufacturing, including 3D metal printing, allowed us to rapidly redesign engine components based on lessons learned through experimentation,” Dr. Kweon, one of the ARL researchers, said to Army.mil. Dr. Kweon further explained that 3D printing allowed them to design an air-cooled engine and ditch a bulky liquid cooling system, reducing the size of the propulsion system. The rapid iteration eventually allowed the researchers to improve fuel atomization and decrease compression leaks.

The heavy-fuel rotary engine doesn’t actually drive the drone’s propellers directly; it uses the engine to spin a 400-volt motor-generator to generate electricity to drive the propeller motors, allowing the engine to spin independently at its most optimal RPM — similar to some hybrid EVs on the road today, except that the engine doesn’t have a mechanical link to the propellers. This system may include a battery for the drone to fly without the engine running; however, the US military has not disclosed much about the VICTOR drone’s battery configuration.

The VICTOR drone is a vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) unmanned aircraft, able to fly without a runway. The US Army has shared a video of its first flight, and the drone is able to land and take off in terrain that would otherwise be impossible for other non-VTOL two-winged aircraft. With a battery system, the drone could cover large distances on a single fuel-up, and air-cooling gives it another layer of robustness, avoiding maintenance on a liquid cooling system.

#10633. Nintendo reports profit is up 11%, but sales slipped for the first half of the fiscal year

Japanese video-game maker Nintendo reported Thursday an 11% improvement in its net profit in the first half of the fiscal year, although its sales declined during that period.

Kyoto-based Nintendo Co.’s April-September profit rose to 220.9 billion yen ($1.4 billion) from nearly 199 billion yen in the same period a year earlier. Sales during the six months slipped 12% to 966 billion yen.

Nintendo, which makes Pokemon, Super Mario and Legend of Zelda games, sold 1.27 million Switch game consoles during the six months, and 6.49 million of its Switch 2 machines, the company said.

In game software, “Star Fox” and “Splatoon Raiders,” released during that period, sold briskly, while earlier releases like “Mario Kart World” were still in demand, it said.

Nintendo’s digital sales, including proceeds from downloadable games, continued to surge. The popularity of “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie,” a 2026 animation film, also boosted its bottom line.

Companies like Nintendo tend to record their biggest sales during the present-giving Christmas and New Year’s seasons.

Nintendo did not break down quarterly details. It kept its projections for the full fiscal year through March 2027 unchanged at 310 billion yen profit, down nearly 27% from the previous fiscal year, on 2 trillion yen in sales, down 11%.

Like other technology companies, Nintendo is facing the problem of a computer chips crunch and surging prices due to the recent global boom in artificial intelligence.

Nintendo stocks rose 6.3% Thursday in Tokyo.

#10631. 7 ways the midterms may affect the AI boom

Welcome to AI Decoded, Fast Company‘s weekly newsletter that breaks down the most important news in the world of AI. I’m Mark Sullivan, a senior writer at Fast Company, covering emerging tech, AI, and tech policy.

Sign up to receive this newsletter every week via email here. And if you have comments on this issue and/or ideas for future ones, drop me a line at sullivan@fastcompany.com, and follow me on X @thesullivan.

There were 41 ballot initiatives limiting data centers; all but one are on track to pass

Voters in 10 states weighed in Tuesday on 41 local ballot measures related to data centers, Forbes reported. Ohio led with 21 measures, followed by Illinois with seven, Maine with four, and Kansas with three. Six other states—California, Florida, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota, and Wisconsin—had one each. Of the measures with reported results, all but one went against data center development, reflecting widespread opposition to the facilities.

In Ohio, voters overwhelmingly backed restrictions on data centers, including outright bans in several municipalities. More than 80% of voters in Ashville rejected an agreement involving two proposed data centers, though the vote does not itself halt construction. In Kansas, Emporia approved a ban on high-impact data centers, while Ottawa voted to prohibit facilities consuming more than 25 megawatts of power. Boulder City, Nevada, rejected a proposal to permit data centers in the Eldorado Valley Transfer Area. One notable exception came in Harwood, North Dakota, where voters rejected a measure that would have required additional review of certain industrial developments, including data centers.

Democrats say AI hearings and legislation are coming

“Two things will change next term,” Representative Ted Lieu of California, vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus, said at a press conference Wednesday. “We will hold public hearings on AI. We will pass legislation, reasonable guardrails, on AI.” Lieu criticized Republicans for failing to regulate the industry while they controlled Congress and said Democrats would also consider restrictions on new data center construction.

The odds of strong AI legislation “just shot up,” Shakeel Hashim wrote in Transformer. He argues that Democrats’ commanding congressional majorities would reduce the need for compromise. If the party wins 56 Senate seats—it currently has 54, with two races uncalled—it would need just four Republicans to overcome a filibuster. Hashim believes that support could be easier to secure as Republicans begin distancing themselves from Trump. Hashim predicts that Congress could within months pass legislation tougher than the bipartisan FRONTIER Act (cosponsored by Jay Obernolte, Republican of California, and Lori Trahan, Democrat of Massachusetts), including mandatory testing and approval of the most powerful artificial intelligence models and tighter limits on federal preemption of state laws.

Stocks rallied on the blue wave

Trump was supposed to be the president Wall Street and the AI industry wanted. Yet markets rallied on news that he had lost control of Congress. Global stocks initially fell as Tuesday’s midterm results trickled in, then rebounded as the scale of the Democratic sweep became clear, The New York Times reports. The S&P 500 closed 1.6% higher on Wednesday. Asian stocks initially tumbled amid fears that Democratic control of Congress would slow the AI buildout. Taiwan Semiconductor fell 1.5%, while SoftBank dropped 3.2%. But those concerns quickly faded. South Korea’s KOSPI reversed course to close up 0.6%, while European and U.S. stocks rallied. As the Times notes, investors have historically welcomed divided government, and the resolution of election uncertainty can matter more to markets than the outcome itself.

CoreWeave, a bellwether for the AI bubble, saw its bonds hit new lows

CoreWeave’s bonds tumbled Wednesday after Democratic candidates who campaigned on slowing data center construction won governorships, Bloomberg reports. Its unsecured debt due in 2031 traded as low as 79.5 cents on the dollar, among the worst performers in high-yield bonds, with its 2030 and 2032 obligations near distressed levels and yields above 15% (issuers must offer higher yields as confidence that the debt will be repaid erodes). In Texas, Gina Hinojosa ousted Greg Abbott to become the state’s first Democratic governor in more than 30 years after repeatedly calling for an immediate moratorium on data centers. Two governors-elect, Amy Acton in Ohio and Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, also ran on slowing construction.

CoreWeave’s stock was already falling. CoreWeave shares had declined approximately 40% over the preceding month as investors grew concerned about the company’s debt, according to Morningstar data. Its bond yields had reached 15% or higher in October, well before the election. The company reports third-quarter results on November 10. Among the questions facing investors is whether rising bond yields have increased CoreWeave’s cost of borrowing, and whether it is bringing new data center capacity online on schedule.

The last constraint on the AI buildout is political

Ben Thompson, a business and tech analyst, argued in his newsletter Stratechery that the main constraint on building more AI data centers will soon have little to do with physical resources. “First we were short on compute, but that ramped; now we are short on memory, but that will ramp; we were coming close to being short on power, but that will be rectified,” Thompson wrote. “The final constraint is political, and that may be the most imposing constraint of all.”

Thompson refers to the public angst over new data center builds that was clearly expressed in the midterms, and he doesn’t expect that angst to lift anytime soon. “This isn’t a partisan issue, where the pendulum will swing back in two years. Both parties see opposition to data centers as a winning cause,” he says, pointing to local officials recalled for approving projects in their own communities. 

A scarcity of compute power could have some unintended, and positive, effects. The fierce competition among frontier AI labs has prevented them from moderating the pace of their research on new models, which, evidence shows, may be outpacing the development of effective safety guardrails. A slowdown might also reduce the terrific amounts of money the labs must spend to reserve computing power in the future, which could improve their overall financial position.

Elon Musk spent $474 million and still lost Texas

Elon Musk poured roughly $474 million into the midterms—nearly twice what he spent helping elect Trump in 2024—and had little to show for it. Of the 106 congressional candidates he backed, 44 lost, including Ken Paxton in Texas. Musk also backed the losing gubernatorial candidates Greg Abbott in Texas and Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio. Just 18 of his congressional candidates had won as of Wednesday, all in seats Republicans were already expected to hold, while 44 races remained uncalled. Musk spent $212 million backing Paxton alone, only to see him lose to James Talarico, the Democrat, by 12 points.

The defeats could have real consequences for Musk’s business empire. Roughly a fifth of SpaceX’s $18.7 billion in 2025 revenue came from federal agencies, and Democrats will soon chair the congressional committees overseeing some of its biggest government customers. Democrats have discussed investigating DOGE, federal contracts involving SpaceX and Tesla, and Starshield’s role in Ukraine. As the Democratic wins piled up Tuesday night, Representative Robert Garcia of California, the incoming House Oversight Committee chair, tweeted simply “LAWYER UP”.

Meanwhile, in Texas, Hinojosa has proposed a moratorium on new data centers and will gain influence over state incentives and the commission that could decide whether to sell Boca Chica State Park to SpaceX. Investors appeared rattled: SpaceX shares fell 3.8% on Wednesday, while Tesla dropped 3.3%.

The AI industry’s biggest donors mostly lost

Democrats turned frustration with the tech industry into a midterm advantage, Politico reported, and, like Musk, Silicon Valley’s biggest donors have little to show for their GOP campaign donations. Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz contributed $116 million, mainly to Republicans. OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, put $50 million primarily into GOP campaigns.

Candidates ran against data centers and won. Much of Silicon Valley’s donation money went toward electing data center-friendly Republicans in Texas and Ohio, states where new facilities are planned. Hinojosa, in Texas, and Sherrod Brown, Ohio’s senator-elect, both ousted Republicans on voter unease about the facilities. Rebecca Cooke used the same playbook in Wisconsin, as did several Pennsylvania Democrats: Paige Cognetti, Bob Brooks, and Bob Harvie. Manny Rutinel, congressman-elect in Colorado’s 8th, made his record on state AI laws central to his campaign. “Allying with the worst parts of the AI industry is just kryptonite for a campaign, and the results tonight double down on that,” said Alex Bores, the New York state lawmaker who got buried by Big Tech money in a U.S. House primary this spring.

#10629. AI Testing Tools: Benefits, Limitations, and Best Practices

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every vendor says the same thing: buy our AI, and testing gets easy. Don't believe it. AI testing tools do help, though. Some teams save real hours with them, while others waste a quarter and a budget. The difference usually comes down to how they start.

They support your QA team by writing test cases, running them, spotting failures and suggesting repairs. Some tools read a requirements document. Others watch real users click around and then replay what they did. Playwright, for instance, now ships built-in test agents: a planner that explores your app and writes a test plan, a generator that turns the plan into test files, and a healer that runs the suite and tries to repair failing tests.

Old-school automation needs a person to write every script. Then a developer moves one button and the whole thing falls over. Somebody loses a morning to repairs, and QA engineers hate that part of the job.

Quality is the big worry. Generated tests can look clever and prove nothing. A tool might confirm that a checkout page opens and then mark checkout as covered, but opening a page is not testing it. Even Playwright's documentation says generated tests may contain initial errors and that you should review what the healer changes before accepting it. A person has to read the output every time.

Business logic is the next problem. The tool has no idea that your refund window dropped from 30 days to 14, and it cannot feel that a signup form is confusing. Intent lives in people's heads.

Coverage numbers can mislead. A dashboard says 90%, and the room relaxes. Meanwhile, the odd edge cases nobody thought of sit untouched. Bugs do not read dashboards.

Check fit first. Does it cover web, mobile and API tests, and does it work with your stack? Ask before any sales call, not after. Then test its honesty: when something fails, a good tool tells you why. A vague red mark costs your team time because nobody can verify it. Read the pricing page slowly, too, since some vendors charge per seat and some per test run.

Finally, throw your ugliest feature at it. Demos use tidy little apps, but your product has pop-ups, slow pages and odd corners. Watch how the tool handles those.

Expecting instant results. People switch the tool on and wait for magic. What they get is noisy reports and grumpy engineers. Some managers even cut QA headcount right away, which is a bad idea: somebody has to tune the tool and handle the cases it cannot. Good testers become more valuable, not less.

Skipping training. Your team needs to learn how the tool behaves. Two short workshops and a shared doc go a long way.

Trusting machine-written text without a second look. AI tools now draft test descriptions, bug reports and release notes too. If your team wants to know how much of a document was machine-generated, an AI-content checker such as ZeroGPT can give a rough signal. Treat the result as a hint rather than proof, because such detectors make mistakes and publish their own accuracy claims.

Agents are the obvious next step. Instead of running fixed scripts, they poke around your app like a curious user, clicking, typing and reporting anything strange. Early versions already exist, and they are rough but improving.

Editors will change as well. Your code editor may soon suggest a test the moment you finish a function, and some bug reports may arrive with a fix attached. The wall between development and QA is getting thin.

Yes, but carefully. AI testing tools will not replace your QA team. They take the boring work off testers' hands and spot patterns people might miss, but they still need a human to say "that result is wrong." Start small, measure what happens and keep your testers close to the tool. Do that, and you will ship faster without losing control.

#10627. ‘Executed for creating an AI poster for your burger restaurant’: Woke 3.0 visions captivate social media

According to social media, this week’s midterms are ushering in a new era: Woke 3.0.

For the uninitiated, the internet has broken down the dynamics of American politics in the 2020s into a few distinct eras. There was Woke 1.0 at the start of the decade, associated with far-left social movements of the time. As the country leaned toward conservatism in the mid-2020s, online denizens argued that Democrats responded by moving into Woke 2.0, a shift that New York City Councilman Chi Ossé defined as “more productive” and less focused on virtue signaling than Woke 1.0.

Now, after the blue tsunami, social media is convinced that a third iteration of Woke might just be upon us. The newfound Democratic majorities in both chambers of Congress have social media anticipating a big cultural swing back to the left, and it’s got plenty of ideas of what that might look like. 

Welcome to Woke 3.0

As soon as Democrats started pulling away with the midterms, concepts for America under Woke 3.0 started going viral.

That includes everything from a rejection of AI (“Under Woke 3.0, you will be publicly executed for creating an AI poster for your burger restaurant,” one user wrote) to a celebration of trans athletes (“Woke 3, we’re having trans athletes swim in the Reflecting Pool,” another user quipped). 

“WOKE 3 IS HERE,” a third user declared. “EVERYONE JUST GOT ANOTHER SET OF PRONOUNS, YOU ARE NOW LEGALLY REQUIRED TO THEY/THEM YOUR DOG.”

One of the most prolific Woke 3.0 posters is an account known as Bald Ann Dowd, who imagined the blue wave bringing everything from universal healthcare “for diseases we don’t even have” to Ramadan-themed Hallmark movies. She even suggested we’re jumping straight to Woke One Billion: “We’re in the club sipping gluten free lean.”

But not everyone on social media was eager to “lib out.” Social media’s dreams of an ultraprogressive government depend on the politicians that are now in power, who may not be quite as eager to swing back to the far left.

One user pointed to a statement by Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), who’s poised to become the next speaker of the House. Jeffries told the press that he’s “ready, willing, and able to find bipartisan common ground” with Republicans, casting doubt on Congress’s willingness to embrace “Woke 3.0.”

“They’re already trying to compromise with a group that wants something diametrically opposed to them,” the user wrote. “Even with a majority, they behave like controlled opposition; being feckless is all they know.”

The new millennial cringe

This summer, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) went viral for saying that “Woke 1 was crazy” on the ABC News show This Week, granting the concept of different eras of “Woke” political legitimacy. AOC’s comment rubbed some people the wrong way, with critics arguing it dismissed the political work of the early 2020s that continues today.

Now, AOC has sounded off on the wave of political optimism spurred by the midterms, saying it reminds her of how it felt when Barack Obama won the presidential election. In a video addressing Gen Z posted on Wednesday night, she encouraged younger Americans to embrace the “earnestness” of so-called “millennial cringe.”

“Imagine all the seats we flipped last night. That feeling, plus, on top of it, electing the first Black president ever. And on top of that, you did it the first time you ever voted,” AOC said. The now-37-year-old was just 19 when Obama was elected president in 2008.

“That hits generationally. Like, you are chasing that feeling ever since,” AOC continued. “And because you did it the first time you ever voted, you’re, like, ‘Yeah, we can change the world. Why not? We did it the first time. Let’s just do it again.’

“That’s so much of it in a nutshell,” she concluded. “Just keep at it.”

That’s the only real cost unless you need something very specific, and Garmin has several subscriptions for somewhat random things.

Garmin’s Vivoactive lineup is made for casual athletes who find themselves running every so often, go to the gym regularly (but aren’t trying to beat Olympic records), and just find workouts to be a healthy part of normal life. Garmin came out with a Vivoactive 6 earlier this year, which retails for $299, and only offers a few advantages that you might care about. And yes, it even supports proper messaging, images, and replies on Android!

Both the Vivoactive 5 and 6 sport the same 11-day battery life, an AMOLED display with 360 x 360 resolution, 5ATM water depth rating, and 23g weight (without the band). The Vivoactive 6 boosts the storage to 8Gb (from 4GB on the Vivoactive 5) and has a new UI, supports Garmin’s Smart Wake feature, and also includes Garmin’s PacePro feature.

Smart Wake is cool, but only people who wear their watch 24/7 will benefit from it. Likewise, running fans may enjoy PacePro, which gives pace guidance throughout a run. I never use offline song downloads for runs, but double the storage could be worth it if you do. If those features aren’t a big deal, this Garmin Vivoactive 5 deal is the best price you’re going to find on a Garmin smartwatch.

The company has been getting away with it for years, too.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Google just shut down a massive botnet operation involving an OEM and ODM manufacturer. According to the company blog, Videostrong Technology Co., which was a certified Android TV partner, purposefully installed a backdoor into 1.3 million set-top boxes and then sold access to criminal affiliates. This allowed for the installation of hidden software that the bad actors could use to conduct ad fraud, build residential proxy networks, and even remotely install malware on the device itself to target the end-user.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the company said in the Google Cloud blog post. It also added, “We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.”

While Google did not mention when Videostrong started loading malware into its products, the company said that the pre-installed malware evolved into a complex, three-stage design in 2024. This meant that the manufacturer has been exploiting millions of devices for years now, with the latest developments designed to make the malware more resilient and allow for multiple bad actors to take advantage of the system. Even though the company has already terminated its business relationship with Videostrong, the open-source nature of Android means that it could continue using the operating system on its products.

There have been supply chain attacks in the past, wherein a third-party compromises a trusted product to steal data, like some Ledger hardware wallets that have been sold by a reseller in Southeast Asia and Europe. Although Google did not characterize this as a supply chain attack, as it was perpetrated by the manufacturer itself and not a third-party operator, it still compromised a supposedly trusted operating system, leading to millions of victims. This incident also shows how even the simplest of devices can be used to execute complicated attacks, like how a Chinese couple hid a PC behind a fridge in a Japanese hotel and targeted 2.4 million victims.

#10622. Richard Branson admits he’s ‘embarrassed’ by other billionaires’ political spending

Virgin Group founder Richard Branson said he is “embarrassed” by other billionaires’ political spending, but added that the results of the U.S. midterm elections sent a “hopeful message about the limits of money in politics.”

“As a successful entrepreneur, I have felt embarrassed by the billions that tech entrepreneurs and hedge fund managers have spent on—mostly Republican—campaigns this election cycle,” the British business magnate posted on LinkedIn yesterday.

“I’m delighted that, finally, U.S. voters stood up to this flood of money and the often hateful and false messages it helped spread,” he said.

Branson added that laws allowing unlimited political spending by individuals and corporations need to change. “I hope this will prompt the next Congress to start a fresh conversation about the toxic impact of money in politics and the need for meaningful campaign finance reform,” he wrote.

Political megadonors poured record-breaking amounts into this year’s midterms. The 40 largest donors spent a combined $2.4 billion through mid-October, according to the Brennan Center for Justice.

While major donors have historically preferred Democrats—in 2014, for example, the top 40 donors favored Democrats 2-to-1—Republican-aligned donors have since surpassed them. GOP donors outspent their left-leaning counterparts more than 3-to-1 during the current cycle. 

Elon Musk was by far the biggest individual player. The Tesla and SpaceX founder poured nearly half a billion dollars into Republican campaigns and super PACs, including a massive investment in Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s unsuccessful Senate bid.

Other major donors included Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, Jeff Yass, Miriam Adelson, and Marc Andreessen on the Republican side, and George Soros and Michael Bloomberg on the Democratic side.

Musk’s preferred candidates suffered steep losses, with Reuters reporting that just three of the 43 Republican House candidates he backed had won, while 33 lost. The remaining results were still outstanding as of late Wednesday.

Six of the seven Senate candidates Musk supported lost, including Paxton in Texas, where he reportedly spent nearly $230 million.
